name: 8-bit tile graphics
summary: A world drawn from 8×8 pixel tiles on a 256×240 screen, with 3 colours plus transparency in each sprite and a fixed hardware palette of about 54 colours. Black outlines and flat fills make each house and tree a small icon.

philosophy.core_thesis: A small grid and a small palette force each object into its clearest silhouette, so a house in 16 pixels reads at once.
design_principles: Build every background from 8×8 or 16×16 tiles that repeat on a grid.
Give each sprite 3 colours plus transparent; outline it in black or a dark hue.
Use flat fills; show volume with one highlight row and one shadow row, never a gradient.
Keep the screen at 256×240 pixels and scale it up with hard nearest-neighbour edges.
Use a sky of one flat colour, often light blue or black.
Make a character 16 to 32 pixels high, with a large head.
anti_patterns: More than 4 colours in one 16×16 area
Perspective that breaks the tile grid

projection_and_camera.camera: Scrolls left and right, or flips screen by screen.
projection_and_camera.framing: About 16 tiles across and 15 down; the ground line sits in the lower third.

geometry.primitive: An 8×8 pixel tile; sprites of 8×8 or 8×16.
geometry.budget: 64 sprites, no more than 8 on one scan line; 256 distinct background tiles.
geometry.edge_rule: Hard pixel steps; diagonals in clean 1:1 or 2:1 runs.
geometry.proportion: A character is 1 to 2 tiles high; a door is 2 tiles; a house front is 4 to 6 tiles.

surface.texture_rule: A brick or a leaf is a 2- or 3-colour pattern inside one tile, repeated.
surface.texel_density: about 16 px for each metre at the scale of the character
surface.filtering: Nearest neighbour; every pixel is a hard square.
surface.material_model: Painted: each material is a fixed tile with its colours in it.

palette.strategy: A fixed hardware palette; each 16×16 area takes one 3-colour sub-palette plus the shared background colour.
palette.colour_depth: a 54-colour master palette, 4 sub-palettes of 3 colours

lighting.model: Painted into the tiles; no light engine.
lighting.shadows: A dark tile row under an object, or none.
lighting.atmosphere: None; the air is clear and flat.
lighting.time_of_day: A swap of the sky colour: light blue for day, black for night.

world_and_space.scale: Doors are twice the height of the character; streets are one screen long.
world_and_space.interiors: A room is a separate screen with a flat back wall, a floor line and furniture as single sprites.
world_and_space.exteriors: A street is a row of house fronts on one ground line, with the sky above.
world_and_space.threshold: Walk into a door and cut to a new screen.

principles.rule: Draw a door 2 tiles high for a character of 1 to 1.5 tiles.
Use 2 planes: background tiles and sprites in front.
Keep the player near the left third of the screen in the scroll direction.

interface.placement: A strip at the top or the bottom, about 10–15% of the screen, on black.
interface.type_and_icons: An 8×8 pixel font in capitals; icons are single tiles.
interface.diegesis: Mostly on top; signs in the world are tiles with no readable text.

emotion.target_response: A bright, toy-like confidence: the viewer reads each thing at once and feels a world small enough to master.

avoid_when: The brief needs depth, light or real material.
The space must feel calm and adult.

modifiers.how: Keep the tiles; widen the palette to 256 colours and add 2 to 4 parallax layers.
Keep the grid; reduce the palette to 4 shades of one hue.

colour_depth.note: A 54-colour master palette, used through 2-bit sub-palettes.
